content: Technology and health innovations will enhance current tools and programs to create practical and affordable solutions that simplify rabies case reporting, management, cost-effectiveness, and accessibility. Existing online resources, such as the Rabies Blueprint and SARE, will be expanded upon, and additional technologies will be developed to support policymakers, scientists, medical professionals, educators, and the general public. Efforts will be made to improve rabies clinical diagnosis through e-learning courses and IT-based assessment tools. Leveraging existing programs, such as toll-free numbers and village reporters, will strengthen decentralized rabies surveillance. Cross-sectoral working groups and regional workshops will facilitate these advancements. The goal is to stimulate innovation in vaccination strategies, diagnostics, and supply chains to address current needs, with a focus on universally applicable and practical tools for resource-limited settings. Enhancing rabies diagnostics will improve disease surveillance in both humans and animals, particularly through laboratory-based tests that require specialized training, equipment, and sample transportation. Through expert stakeholder consultations, support will be sought from the community of practice, and collaboration with countries, academia, and industry will help establish clear research priorities for rabies diagnostic tests. Laboratory manuals will be updated to provide harmonized and current guidance for human and animal rabies diagnosis, following established WHO and OIE processes. Practical regional workshops will be conducted to train personnel in rabies surveillance and diagnosis. Accurate and comprehensive monitoring of new rabies cases will enable progress assessment, validation of rabies-free status, and targeted interventions in affected areas. Best-practice surveillance systems for human and animal rabies will be clarified, and tools for monitoring and reporting data will be refined. Regional workshops will build surveillance capacity, share successes and lessons learned, and support the development of locally appropriate surveillance systems. Globally, integrated reporting systems for human and animal surveillance data will be promoted to create a coordinated understanding of the rabies disease burden and the impact of interventions. Reporting results and program impacts will help identify effective interventions, demonstrate return on investment, and assess progress toward goals. Countries will be supported in collecting and reporting program data, forecasting vaccine needs, assessing performance, and targeting elimination strategies. Processes will be established to validate and verify progress toward zero human rabies deaths, and guidance will be developed for last-mile strategies and maintaining elimination once achieved. Activities from 2017 to 2020 aim to design and disseminate information on surveillance and data collection tools, improve rabies surveillance tools, and organize regional workshops to train technical staff in best practices. Integrated regional and global reporting systems for human and animal rabies data will be established, along with clear reporting chains within human and veterinary health services. Regular programmatic monitoring at national and regional levels will use surveillance data to demonstrate the impact of investments in rabies elimination. Processes for validation and verification of zero human rabies deaths will be established. Advocacy efforts will highlight the feasibility of rabies elimination, promote prioritization within countries, and support the development of advocacy materials and strategies that emphasize the global public good of rabies elimination. Countries will be supported in synergizing rabies elimination programs with other healthcare interventions to strengthen health systems and improve outcomes for other diseases. Guidance will be provided on approaching development partners for financing, enabling countries to implement local programs to achieve elimination goals. Sustained financing is essential to plan, implement, and maintain rabies elimination activities. Existing models for vaccine forecasting and investments will be adapted to identify and predict resource needs. Program outcomes will be used to advocate for investment and establish clear resource mobilization strategies. Countries will be supported in obtaining and investing their own funds in rabies elimination activities to ensure ownership and success. Evaluating activities will allow refinement and improvement of implementation in subsequent countries and phases. Financing strategies for activities described in the logic framework are detailed in the budget. Collaboration with experienced external fundraisers will generate investment in elimination and seek additional financing for initial stock for rabies biological banks. Synergies with other programs and innovative funding mechanisms will be explored. Results and impacts of the United Against Rabies collaboration will be regularly monitored and reported to key stakeholders. The phased approach to funding Zero by 30 involves three phases: Start-Up (2018–2020), Scale-Up (2021–2025), and Mop-Up (2026–2030). Phase 1 focuses on building a strong foundation for rabies elimination by preparing normative tools and structures to catalyze action. Countries with the greatest chance of success will be engaged first, including those where rabies is a priority disease, those already active in rabies control, and those with pilot projects. Developing national and regional rabies elimination plans is a core activity of Phase 1. Anchoring rabies control within national programs ensures country ownership and a sustainable approach adapted to local conditions. Support will be provided to countries to prepare their plans and facilitate their integration into a coordinated regional effort to achieve the global goal of Zero by 30. Phase 2 will expand efforts to engage most endemic countries in rabies elimination, building on the foundation established in Phase 1. Support for countries engaged in Phase 1 will continue, promoting sustainable national programs while engaging new countries. Regional elimination plans will be emphasized, mobilizing countries to implement strategies for their regions. Phase 3 will engage remaining countries in the fight to eliminate rabies, supporting efforts as communities, nations, and regions advance toward the goal. Lessons learned in Phases 1 and 2 will be critical to ensuring success in this final phase. Achievements from the first two phases will be capitalized on to make Zero by 30 a reality. The United Against Rabies collaboration proposes establishing a Global Steering Group (GSG) comprising representatives from WHO, OIE, FAO, and GARC. This agile core unit will respond to changing environments and needs. The GSG will link the global strategic plan to a work plan with clear roles and responsibilities among partners, taking programmatic, financial, and resource decisions related to delivering the global work plans. Mass dog rabies vaccination campaigns, such as those in Payatas, Manila, demonstrate the importance of coordinated efforts. Countries are at the core of the global strategic plan, and their engagement is essential to achieving the goal of Zero by 30.
